3. The plaintiff's case in short is that the plaintiff No. 1 imported two consignments one of 499.446 metric tons of inedible tallow and other of 1,448.819 metric tons of inedible tallow both covered by Invoice No. 1077 dated 6-12-1992 of M/s Kerry (New Zealand) Ltd, Auckland, New Zealand. The said consignment of 499.446 metric tons of inedible tallow and 1,448.819 metric tons of inedible tallow in bulk were shipped at the port of Auckland/Port-land/Fremantle, New Zealand under Tanker Bill of Lading No.ANT/11/92/CGP-O dated 6-12-1992 for carriage to and delivery at Chittagong port per 'Motor Tanker Antares VII' belonging to the defendant, No.1 of which the defendant No.3 is the local agent at Chittagong. The carrying Tanker, 'MT Antares VII' with the consignments in suit arrived at the port of Chittagong on or about 6-1-1993 and took her berth at River Mooring No.3 of the Chittagong Port on 9-1-1993 and discharged her cargo on 9-1-1993 and 10-1-1993 into the shore tanks, Customs Bonded Warehouse of the defendant No.4 under the constant strict supervision of the surveyor appointed by the concerned par-ties and on completion of discharge of the cargo from the carrying motor tanker into the shore tanks, the surveyor issued their survey report to their respective appointing authorities about the quantity delivered from the vessel into the shore tanks. As per the survey report dated 16-1-1993 of the surveyor Messrs NA Survey and Inspection Co. Ltd a quantity of 496.032 metric tons out of 499.446 metric tons and 1420.232 metric tons out of 1448.819 metric tons of inedible tallow in bulk were received at the shore tanks of M/s. International Tank Terminal (Bangladesh) Ltd, since re-named as M/s Van Ommeren Tank Terminal Bangladesh Ltd (defendant No.4) with a shortage of 3.414 metric tons and 28.587 metric tons out of the total consignments 499.446 metric tons and 448.819 metric tons in the suit respectively. Due to short receipt of 32.001 (3.44 + 28.587) metric tons of inedible tallow in bulk out of the two consignments in the suit the plaintiff No.1 suffered a loss of Taka 7,40,538.36. The defendants are liable for the shortages and are bound to compensate the loss sustained by the plaintiff No. 1. The consignments were insured with the plaintiff No. 2. The plaintiff No. 1 having lodged its claim with the plaintiff No. 2 as insurer of the suit cargo and as per terms of the insurance policy, the plaintiff No. 2 has paid a sum of Taka 3,55,324 to the plaintiff No. 1 who in consideration of such payment executed a Letter of Subrogation subrogating and abandoning all of its rights, title and interest in the short dis-charged cargo upto the extent of the amount so paid in favour of the plaintiff No. 2. The plaintiff lodged claim to the defendants for the short delivery of 32 metric tons out of the two consignments of inedible tallow. Since the claim of the plaintiff has not been settled by the defendants in spite of repeated demands the plaintiffs were obliged to institute the instant suit. 

 4. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and the defendant No. 4 contested the suit by filing two separate written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. In the written statement of the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 it is contended that on arrival of the carrying motor tanker at the port of Chittagong an ullage survey was conducted on board the vessel before the discharge of the cargo in presence of the surveyors appointed by the plaintiffs, defendants and all concerned parties together with the customs officials and as per the ullage survey report a quantity of 1942.281 metric tons of tallow was found board the vessel that is only 5.984 metric tons were found allegedly short out of the two consignments as such 1942.281 metric tons of tallow were discharged in full into the shore tanks of the defendant No.4 from the carrying motor tanker by hose pipe connection. After completion of discharge of the cargo into the shore tanks, all the surveyors inspected the carrying vessel's tanks and issued a Dryness Certificate and a Discharge Certificate confirming that there was no cargo left at the carrying vessel's tanks which were found dry. The defendant No.4 also issued a letter to the surveyor of the plaintiff No. 1 stating that the entire cargo was discharged into the shore tanks. The further case of these defendants is that the carriers are entitled to 1% ocean allowance in carrying oil and such kind of cargo as per provisions of law and intention-al trade and practice. The Customs Authority of Bangladesh also allow 1% ocean allowance. So these defendants cannot be held in any way liable for the alleged shortage, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 8. In support of its case, the plaintiff examined one witness. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 did not examine any witness. The documents of the plaintiff were marked as Exhibit-1 Power of Attorney dated 20-3-1997, Exhibit-2 Invoices, Exhibit-3.Bills of lading dated 6-12-1992, Exhibit-4 Survey report dated 28-1-2093 issued by NA Survey and Inspection Co Ltd., Exhibit-5 Shore tank survey report, Exhibit-6 letter dated 27-1-1993 from the plaintiff No.1 to the defendant No.3, Exhibit 6(Ka) letter dated 24-2-1993 from the defendant No.3 to the plain-tiff No. 1, Exhibit 6(Kha) letter dated 1-3-1993, Exhibit 6(Ga) letter dated 22-4-1993 from the plaintiff No. 1 to the defendant No.3, Exhibit 6(Gha) letter dated 20-11-1993 from the plaintiff No.1 to the defendant No.3, Exhibit 7 letter dated 20-11-1993 from the plaintiff No. 1 to the defendant No.3, Exhibit 7(Ka) letter dated 15-7-1993 from the defendant No.3 to the plaintiff No.1; Exhibit 7(Kha) letter dated 24-2-1993 from the defendant No. 3 to the plaintiff No.1 and Exhibit 8, Marine Certificate of Insurance. 

 10. The learned Advocate appearing for the Appellants submits that after arrival of the carrying motor tanker at the port of Chittagong and prior to commencing the discharge of the cargo an ullage survey was conducted on board the vessel in presence of the surveyors appointed by the plaintiffs, defendants and all concerned parties together with the customs officials and as per the aforesaid ullage survey report a quantity of 1942.281 metric tons of tallow were found on board the vessel i.e. 5.984metric tons of tallow were found allegedly short out of the total consignment of 1948.265 metric tons of tallow which was discharged in full into the shore tanks of the defendant No.4 from the carrying motor tanker by hose pipe connection; that after discharge of the cargo all the surveyors inspected the carrying vessel's tanks and issued Dryness Certificate and Discharge Certificate confirming that there was no cargo left at the carrying vessel's tanks and the tanks were found to be empty and dry. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that the Court below erred in law in holding the appellant defendants liable for the alleged shortage of the cargo although the cargo of allow was of evaporating nature and the carrier is not at all liable for any alleged shortage under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925. He also submits that the carrier is entitled to 1% ocean allowance as inevitable loss while carrying the cargo of tallow and accordingly the appellants cannot be saddled with any liability whatsoever for any alleged shortage. The learned Advocate for the Appellant further submits that the trial Court erred in law in holding the appellant defendants liable on the basis of shore tanks figures although they had discharged the cargo in full and that in case of conflict between the shore tank survey and ullage survey carried out on board the vessel prior to discharge of the cargo, the ullage survey report will prevail over the shore tank figures survey report and in support of his submission he cited the decisions reported in 61 DLR 801, 15 BLC 737 and 9 BLC 218 that the trial Court ought to have considered that the appellant/defendants are not liable for the alleged shortage of cargo and, as such, the decree passed by the trial Court cannot be sustained. 

 13. It appears that one Mr Prodip Mojumder is the attorney of the plaintiff No. 1. He as PW1 has deposed that the plaintiff No. 1 imported two consignments one of 499.446 metric tons and another of 1448.819 metric tons of tallow in bulk from Auckland, New Zealand and the said cargo was shipped in motor tanker belonging to the defendant Nos.1, 2 and 3 and the carrying motor tanker arrived at the port of Chittagong on 9-1-1993 and discharged her cargo on 9-1-1993 and 10-1-1993 into the shore tanks of the defendant No. 4 under the constant strict supervision of the surveyors appointed by the concerned parties and in presence of the customs officials. He further deposed that a quantity of 32.001 metric tons of tallow were short discharged from the carrying motor tanker and, as such, the plaintiff No.1 suffered a total loss of Taka 7,40,538.36. PW1 in his cross-examination stated that they have taken delivery of the cargo from the defendant No.4 and the PW1 did not know whether the defendant No. 4 is liable for the alleged loss of the plaintiff or not. PW1 further stated in his cross-examination that he was not present at the joint survey at the terminal, that they have taken the delivery of the cargo from the tank terminal and not from the vessel, that they have received less cargo from the tank terminal, that he was not present when the surveyors signed their respective survey reports, that it is stated in the bill of lading that the vessel is not liable for the quantity, measurement, weight, quality, nature and the value of the cargo. He denied the suggestion that the imported cargo of the plaintiff No. 1 was discharged in full into the shore tanks from the carrying motor tanker. 

 14. These are all the evidences adduced by the parties. We have heard the learned Advocate for the appellants at length and perused the materials on record including the pleadings and deposition of PW1 and the Exhibits. It appears from the materials on record that the plaintiff No. 1 imported the 499.446 metric tons and another of 1448.81 metric tons of tallow in bulk totaling 1948.265 metric tons of tallow in bulk from Auckland, New Zealand and the vessel 'MT Antares VII' carried the cargo. The defendant No.1 is the owner of the vessel, the defendant No.2 is the despondent owner of the vessel, the defendant No.3 is the local agent of the vessel. The vessel 'MT Antares VII' arrived at the port of Chittagong on 6-1-1993 and took her berth on 9-1-1993 and discharged her cargo on 9-1-1993 and 10-1-1993 into the shore tanks of the defendant No.4 under the constant strict supervision of the surveyors appointed by the concerned parties. It appears that as per the survey report dated 28-1-1993 carried out by NA Survey and Inspection Co Ltd (Exhibit 4) after arrival of the vessel at the port of Chittagong and prior to dis-charge of the cargo an ullage survey was conducted on 9-1-1993 on board the vessel 'MT Antares VII' in presence of the surveyors appointed by all the parties concerned and as per the ullage survey a quantity of 1942.281 metric tons of tallow in bulk were found on board the vessel i.e. 5.984 metric tons were found allegedly short out of the total consignment of 1948.265 metric tons of tallow. But as per the shore tank survey report (Exhibit 5) a quantity of 32.001 metric tons of tallow was short discharged from the vessel 'MT Antares VII' into the shore tanks of the defendant No.4. 

 15. It may be reiterated that at the time of making his submission, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs cited three decisions of this Court as mentioned above of which in the case of Erria Shipping Pvt Ltd and another vs Lever Brothers (Bangladesh) Ltd reported in 61 DLR 801, the case of Botany Bay Parcel Tankers International and another vs Lever Brothers Bangladesh Ltd and another reported in 15 BLC 737 and the case of Lever Brothers Bangladesh Ltd vs Botany Bay Shipping Co (Rust) Pvt Ltd and another reported in 9 BLC 218 it has been held that in the event of conflict between 2(two) reports one by ullage survey report and the other by shore tank survey report the ullage survey report must prevail over the shore tank survey report. It has also been held in the case reported in 61 DLR 801 as mentioned above that the carriers are entitled to 1% ocean allowance in the carriage of bulk cargo like oil. As per the ullage survey report there was an alleged shortage of 5.984 metric tons of tallow. As per international trade and practice the carrier is entitled to 1% ocean allowance as inevitable loss while carrying bulk cargo like oil/tallow and, as such, the aforesaid shortage of 5.984 metric tons of tallow. As per international trade and practice the carrier is entitled to 1% ocean allowance as inevitable loss while carrying bulk cargo like oil/ tallow and, as such, the aforesaid shortage of 5.984 is well covered by 1% ocean allowance allowed as per international trade and practice.
